blocks.content: Disk scheduling reuses a familiar word, scheduling, from earlier in this course, but applies it to a completely different resource. This chapter is not about which process gets the CPU next, it is about the order in which a spinning hard disk services a queue of pending read and write requests, a decision that has a real, measurable effect on performance because moving the physical read write head is slow.

Every algorithm here answers the exact same question with a different strategy: given a head currently sitting at some position and a queue of pending requests scattered across the disk, in what order should they be serviced to keep total head movement, and therefore total wasted time, as low as possible.
1. Why Order Matters: The Physical Cost of a Seek
blocks.text: 1. Why Order Matters: The Physical Cost of a Seek

blocks.content: On a traditional spinning hard disk, reading or writing data at a given location requires physically moving a mechanical arm so its read write head sits above the correct track, called seeking, and then waiting for the platter to rotate until the right sector passes underneath, called rotational latency. Only after both of those have happened does the actual data transfer take place.

Seek time is, by a wide margin, the slowest of these three components, since it involves genuine mechanical movement of a physical arm across the surface of a spinning disk. This is exactly why the order in which a batch of pending requests gets serviced matters: servicing them in a scattered, inefficient order forces the head to travel back and forth across the disk far more than necessary, while a smarter order can dramatically cut that total travel distance.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409195654-168165794.png

blocks.title: A note on terminology
blocks.content: This chapter reuses the word scheduling from CPU scheduling earlier in this course, but for an entirely different resource. CPU scheduling decides which process gets processor time next; disk scheduling decides which pending I/O request gets serviced next, and it is fundamentally about minimizing physical arm movement, not fairness among processes.
2. The Shared Example Used Throughout This Chapter
blocks.text: 2. The Shared Example Used Throughout This Chapter

blocks.content: To compare algorithms meaningfully, every example in this chapter uses the exact same setup: the head currently sitting at track 50, and a pending request queue of tracks 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67, arriving in that order. Each algorithm below is applied to this identical queue so the total head movement each one produces can be compared directly and fairly.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409195654-249726097.png
blocks.alt: The Shared Example Used Throughout This Chapter

blocks.content: 3. First Come First Served, FCFS

FCFS disk scheduling services requests in the exact order they arrived in the queue, with no regard at all for where they physically sit relative to the head or to each other. It is the simplest possible policy, and it is perfectly fair in the sense that no request can ever be skipped over indefinitely.

Applying it to the shared example, the head visits 98, then 183, then 37, then 122, then 14, then 124, then 65, then 67, in exactly that order. The honest weakness is immediately visible just from the numbers: the head swings from 50 up to 183, then all the way back down to 37, then back up to 124, a lot of wasted travel purely because requests happened to arrive in a scattered order.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409195654-856572009.png
4. Shortest Seek Time First, SSTF

SSTF takes a greedy approach instead: at every step, it services whichever pending request is physically closest to the head current position, regardless of arrival order. This generally produces noticeably less total head movement than FCFS, since the head is always making the locally cheapest move available.

Applying it to the same queue, from 50 the closest pending request is 37, distance 13. From 37 the closest remaining request is 14, distance 23. From there the closest is 65, then 67, then 98, then 122, then 124, then finally 183. The honest weakness here is fairness: a request sitting far away from the bulk of the traffic can be repeatedly passed over by newer, closer arriving requests, a real form of starvation.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409195654-122559665.png

blocks.title: SSTF starvation, concretely
blocks.content: Imagine a request sitting at track 400 while a steady stream of new requests keeps arriving near track 50. Under pure SSTF, that distant request can be pushed further and further back indefinitely, since something closer to the head is always available first. This is exactly the same starvation idea covered in the CPU scheduling module, just applied to disk requests instead of processes.
5. SCAN, the Elevator Algorithm

SCAN fixes SSTF fairness problem with a simple physical rule: the head moves in one direction, sweeping across the disk and servicing every pending request it passes along the way, all the way to one physical end of the disk, and only then reverses direction and sweeps back the other way.

The standard mental model for this is an elevator in a building: it does not jump erratically between floors based on which button was pressed first, it travels in one direction, stopping at every floor with a waiting passenger along the way, reaches the top, and then comes back down the same way, stopping again as needed. SCAN behaves identically, just with disk tracks in place of floors.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409195654-620660943.png

Applying SCAN to the shared example, moving toward the high end first from 50, the head passes through 65, 67, 98, 122, 124, 183, continues to the physical end of the disk at track 199 even though nothing is pending there, then reverses and picks up 37 and 14 on the way back down.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409195655-779587778.png
6. C-SCAN, Circular SCAN

C-SCAN refines SCAN with one important change: instead of reversing direction and servicing requests on the way back, the head sweeps in one direction only, and upon reaching the end of the disk, it jumps immediately back to the starting end and begins another one directional sweep from there.

The reason for this specific change is fairness at the disk edges. Under plain SCAN, the middle of the disk effectively gets serviced twice per full cycle, once on the way out and once on the way back, while requests sitting near the very ends only get one chance per cycle. C-SCAN treats the disk as circular instead, giving every region of the disk a uniform, predictable wait time regardless of where it physically sits.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409195655-974261239.png
7. LOOK and C-LOOK: A Practical Refinement
blocks.text: 7. LOOK and C-LOOK: A Practical Refinement

blocks.content: Both SCAN and C-SCAN, as described so far, always travel all the way to the physical end of the disk before reversing or jumping back, even if no pending request actually sits out there. LOOK and C-LOOK fix exactly this waste: they only travel as far as the last real pending request in the current direction, then reverse or jump immediately, without continuing on to the true physical end of the disk for no reason.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409197366-40690685.png

9. Why This Matters Far Less on SSDs
blocks.text: 9. Why This Matters Far Less on SSDs

blocks.content: Every algorithm in this chapter exists to solve one specific physical problem: minimizing the movement of a mechanical read write head across a spinning platter. A solid state drive, covered in full in the dedicated SSD vs HDD chapter, has no mechanical arm and no seek time at all, access latency is essentially uniform regardless of where on the drive the data physically sits.

This means classic disk scheduling algorithms provide little to no real benefit on modern SSDs, and are increasingly a legacy concern tied specifically to spinning HDDs. They remain, however, one of the most reliably asked topics in OS interviews, precisely because tracing through a request queue by hand exercises a genuinely useful skill: reasoning carefully about physical resource contention.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409197367-143321734.png
blocks.alt: Why This Matters Far Less on SSDs

blocks.content: 10. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Confusing this physical disk arm scheduling with CPU process scheduling just because of the shared word scheduling, they optimize completely different resources.","Assuming SCAN and C-SCAN behave identically, when their fairness characteristics at the disk edges genuinely differ, SCAN double services the middle per cycle, C-SCAN treats the whole disk uniformly.","Forgetting that SSTF, despite its strong average case performance, carries a real starvation risk that FCFS structurally cannot have."]
items: Confusing this physical disk arm scheduling with CPU process scheduling just because of the shared word scheduling, they optimize completely different resources.
Assuming SCAN and C-SCAN behave identically, when their fairness characteristics at the disk edges genuinely differ, SCAN double services the middle per cycle, C-SCAN treats the whole disk uniformly.
Forgetting that SSTF, despite its strong average case performance, carries a real starvation risk that FCFS structurally cannot have.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to compute total head movement by hand for FCFS, SSTF, and SCAN given a sample request queue and starting head position, exactly like the worked example in this chapter. This is one of the most classic OS interview exercises, and being fluent with the arithmetic, not just the concept, is what separates a strong answer from a shaky one.

This closes the discussion of how the operating system orders competing requests to physical storage. The next chapter turns to the storage medium itself, comparing the mechanical HDD this whole chapter has been built around against the fundamentally different SSD.
